newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians abandon traditional Mamma, Papa plus kids.
newsitem.headline: Italians abandon traditional Mamma, Papa plus kids.

text.p: A social earthquake has shaken Italy, where the family is the traditional bedrock of society.

For the first time, fewer than 50 percent of households are composed of mamma, papa plus the bambini, says a major study by the national statistics institute ISTAT into the structure of Italian society.
Instead, childless couples, one parent families and the number of adults living alone are all on the rise.
The study, published this week, showed a rapid decline in the traditional nuclear family. In 1994, 48 percent of households had children compared to 52.1 percent in 1988.
Big families also appeared to be out. The study showed that among married couples raising a family, nearly 44 percent had only one child.
Men or women who stayed single accounted for 21.1 percent of households in 1994, up from 19.3 percent six years earlier.
The role of the powerful mother who stayed at home to raise the children has also undergone a transformation in Roman Catholic Italy, which now has one of the world's lowest birth rates.
According to ISTAT, both partners worked in 28.6 percent of families and women were housewives in only a third of cases.
But it said both partners worked in two-thirds of families in the affluent north while 54.4 percent of women stayed at home in the conservative south and nearly 60 percent in the islands.
The figures confirmed Italians were increasingly choosing not to have children -- the number of childless couples rose to 4.3 million in 1994 against 3.9 million in 1988.
The number of families with three or more children slid to 13.7 percent from 16.2 percent while one child was the norm in 43.8 percent of families compared with 41.0 percent in 1988.
The Roman Catholic Church said the ISTAT study provided evidence of a grave crisis in the Italian family.

"In other countries, such as France for example, where various measures have been taken to support the family, the number of births is on the rise," said Bassano Staffieri, secretary of the Italian Episcopal Commission for the Family.
"Here it's hard enough for a family to live with just one child. How can we expect them to have a second one?" he said.
The study, however, showed no change in Italians' traditional reluctance to leave home.
ISTAT said 80 percent of Italian children stayed at home until they were aged 24.
